title: Where a low-fidelity transonic method stops being trustworthy
subtitle: NASA Common Research Model wing-body · M∞ 0.80-0.85 · Re 5-30×10⁶
thesis: For a fixed numerical treatment the solver's limit is a shock strength, not an angle of attack — and once you know that, you can move it.
credit: VFP is licensed to Cranfield University. The analysis, campaign and conclusions presented here are the author's own; the solver itself is not distributed.

paragraphs: Conceptual aircraft design runs on low-fidelity aerodynamics. A full-potential method coupled to an integral boundary layer returns a transonic wing solution in seconds where RANS takes hours, which is what makes it usable inside a design loop at all. The price is that it holds only while its assumptions hold — and the assumptions fail long before the solver announces it.

On the NASA Common Research Model wing-body, incidence sweeps simply stopped. Somewhere between 3.4° and 3.8°, depending on Mach and Reynolds number, the solver quit. The obvious question is whether that is the method reaching a physical limit or the numerics failing early. They demand opposite responses: the first means believe the answer and stop, the second means fix the setup and continue.
This study answers that question for the CRM, and then does something more useful than answering it. It removes most of the limit.

items.label: Spread in pre-shock Mach at failure

blocks.text: The limit is a shock strength wearing an angle of attack's clothing

paragraphs: The CRM cruises at M∞ = 0.85, and at that freestream Mach number most of the upper surface is supersonic. The critical pressure coefficient — the value of Cp at which local flow first reaches sonic conditions — is only −0.302 at M∞ = 0.85 and −0.435 at M∞ = 0.80. Those are shallow thresholds, exceeded over most of the chord at even modest incidence. The flow is supercritical throughout the useful range, so the supersonic region has to be terminated by a shock.

A shock imposes an essentially discontinuous adverse pressure gradient on the boundary layer beneath it. Whether the layer survives that interaction depends principally on the shock's strength, which for a normal shock is set entirely by the Mach number immediately ahead of it. The static pressure ratio rises steeply: 1.25 at M₁ = 1.1, 1.51 at 1.2, 1.81 at 1.3. The empirical result that matters here is Pearcey's — a turbulent boundary layer separates at the foot of the shock once M₁ reaches roughly 1.3.

blocks.caption: Static pressure ratio across a normal shock. The steepness of this relation in M₁ is why shock strength, rather than incidence, turns out to be the governing quantity.

paragraphs: So the test is straightforward. Take the four archived operating conditions, all run with identical numerics, and ask what the solver has in common at the last incidence it manages. If the answer is an angle, the limit is about incidence. If it is a shock strength, the limit is about the physics of the interaction.

blocks.caption: The failure boundary expressed two ways. As an incidence it scatters across 0.4°; as the peak pre-shock Mach number reached at the last converged incidence it collapses to within 0.061 — and lands on the empirical separation threshold.

blocks.title: The failure boundary collapses onto shock strength
blocks.body: Incidence at failure varies from 3.4° to 3.8°. Peak pre-shock Mach number at failure varies only from 1.310 to 1.371, with three of the four conditions agreeing to within 0.011 — and that band sits on the M₁ ≈ 1.3 separation threshold established from wind tunnel measurement decades earlier. For a fixed numerical treatment, this is a shock-strength boundary, not an incidence boundary.

paragraphs: The supporting evidence lines up. A discrete shock first forms at α = 2.4° and marches forward to roughly 55% chord by α = 3.4°, by which point 57% of the chord is supersonic. Beneath it the boundary layer is in trouble: the shape factor exceeds 2 at 14 of 20 spanwise stations aft of the shock, and skin friction collapses to 7×10⁻⁵. Independently, the NASA NTF measurements place the separation in the same half-degree — the measured lift slope breaks down and the pitching moment bottoms out at α = 3.39°.
The solver, in other words, is not failing early. It is stopping at roughly the point where the flow genuinely leaves the class of flows an integral boundary-layer method can describe.

blocks.text: That threshold is not a property of the flow alone

paragraphs: This is where the study stops being a post-mortem. The italicised qualifier above — for a fixed numerical treatment — is load-bearing. The boundary layer responds to the shock the solver has captured, and a full-potential solver does not capture the real shock. It captures a discrete approximation to it, and how sharp that approximation is depends on the difference scheme.

A campaign of 223 further runs swept the flow-file parameters. Most did nothing. Two moved the limit, and they act by entirely different mechanisms — which is the part that makes the result trustworthy rather than a lucky setting.

blocks.caption: Highest converged incidence over the IOPT1(8) × EPS grid at M∞ = 0.85, Re = 19.8×10⁶. Baseline is IOPT1(8) = 1 with EPS = 0.70.

paragraphs: EPS turns out not to change the answer at all — only whether the relaxation can find it. Across the whole EPS range at fixed scheme, the converged lift coefficient moves by at most 0.00036, or 0.072%, over the eighteen incidences every chain reaches. Over that same range the attainable incidence moves from 3.4° to 5.2°. The failure modes corroborate it: at low EPS the runs die silently without a force summary, the signature of a relaxation that never converged; at high EPS they die instead in the boundary-layer routines. Raising EPS removes the convergence-failure path and exposes the real one underneath.

The difference scheme does change the answer. Between the two schemes the converged lift differs by up to 0.058, or 8.9%, at α = 5.0° — two orders of magnitude more than the EPS sensitivity — and the change is localised at the shock. The non-conservative scheme produces a pressure gradient at the shock foot 30-45% shallower: 6.20 against 9.02 at α = 3.4°, 10.15 against 13.06 at α = 5.0°. The pre-shock Mach number is almost unchanged between them, 1.403 against 1.412 at α = 5.0°. It is the same supersonic region, terminated by a shock spread over more of the chord.

And the boundary layer feels exactly that. Up to α ≈ 4.4° the two schemes give an identical shape-factor history. Beyond it they part company: with the blended scheme the peak shape factor aft of the shock runs away to 2.82 at 4.6° and 4.78 at 5.0°, far outside the range where a two-parameter integral profile family means anything, while with the non-conservative scheme it stays between 2.3 and 2.6 all the way to 5.8°.

blocks.title: The solver does not fail because the incidence is high
blocks.body: It fails because the shock it has captured drives the boundary-layer method outside its representable range. Across the ten branches tested, the shock gradient at a fixed incidence of 3.4° correlates with how far each setting subsequently marches, at −0.77.

blocks.text: An isentropic equation cannot make an entropy jump

paragraphs: Preferring a non-conservative scheme needs justifying, because conservative differencing is normally the more defensible choice. The reason here is specific to the full-potential formulation. The potential equation assumes isentropic, irrotational flow, and therefore cannot represent the entropy rise a real shock produces. A conservative discretisation enforces mass conservation across the discontinuity inside that isentropic framework, and the captured shock comes out stronger than the real one — increasingly so as the shock strengthens. Non-conservative differencing introduces a truncation error that acts, in effect, in place of the missing entropy loss.
That account makes a falsifiable prediction: at high incidence the blended scheme should over-predict the measured pressure rise across the shock, and the non-conservative scheme should not.

blocks.title: The prediction holds
blocks.body: Below α ≈ 4° the two schemes are indistinguishable against the NTF surface pressures, and the tap spacing of 0.05-0.30 chord is too coarse to separate them anyway. Above 4° they diverge. At the two highest measured incidences, 5.07° and 5.08°, the blended scheme over-predicts the pressure rise by +0.099 and +0.096 — about 27% — while the non-conservative scheme sits within −0.017 and −0.021.

blocks.alt: Absolute lift error against incidence for both difference schemes, with the separated range shaded.
blocks.caption: Absolute lift error against NTF Test 215 Run 159 for both schemes at EPS = 0.95. They are equivalent while the flow is attached and diverge once it separates — which is the signature of a real physical mechanism rather than a tuned constant.
Mean absolute lift error against NTF Test 215 Run 159, separated into attached and separated ranges. The cost of the selected setting is visible in the middle column and is stated rather than buried.

paragraphs: The selected setting marches 71% further and halves the lift error where the flow is separated. It is also very slightly worse in the attached range — 0.0188 against 0.0172, a difference of 0.0016 in C_L. That is a real cost and it belongs in the summary, not a footnote. It is worth paying because the attached range was never where the method was in doubt.

The range gain and the accuracy gain have the same cause. That is what separates this from a numerical expedient: a setting that bought extra incidence while degrading the answer would be a way of not knowing, dressed as a fix.

blocks.caption: Lift curve for the baseline and selected settings against NASA NTF Test 215 Run 159. The selected setting both marches further and tracks the measurement more closely once the flow separates.

blocks.text: Four ways to stop, and only one of them says so

paragraphs: Across 587 runs the solver stopped in four distinguishable ways, and the vendor documentation describes only the first.

A divergence abort raises an explicit error — and was never once observed in this campaign. A Fortran runtime crash from the boundary-layer routines is what actually dominates, once EPS is high enough for the relaxation to converge. Silent non-convergence completes the iteration cap and writes no force summary at all. Immediate rejection terminates in about eleven seconds having written only banner lines.

The distinction between the second and third is not cosmetic — it is the evidence that EPS and the difference scheme act on different failure paths. It also has a blunt operational consequence: any automated sweep has to detect all four, because only one announces itself, and it needs a wall-clock cap, because a fifth mode was observed on a separate configuration where the run simply never terminated.

blocks.title: The same solver, the opposite conclusion
blocks.body: A companion study on the SAAB 340 reached the reverse finding: there the method stopped with the boundary layer still attached, at roughly 68% of expected maximum lift, and moving the viscous coupling switch recovered range at no cost in fidelity. Same solver, opposite diagnosis. What separates them is where the limiting adverse-gradient feature sits relative to the coupling switch — a leading-edge suction peak forward of it in the subcritical case, a shock aft of it here. Neither result generalises without that context, which is exactly why 'my solver crashed at 3.4°' is never a finding on its own.

blocks.text: What this means if you use one of these methods

paragraphs: The specific parameter names belong to one solver. The structure of the argument does not, and applies to any coupled full-potential or transonic small-disturbance method with an integral boundary layer — MSES, VGK, TSFOIL and their relatives.

First: when a low-fidelity transonic method stops, check the pre-shock Mach number before checking the incidence. If it sits near 1.3 the flow has probably left the representable class, and no amount of solver configuration will honestly extend the sweep.

Second: that threshold is not fixed. It depends on how sharply your discretisation captures the shock, and a scheme that spreads the shock over more chord will march further. Whether it should is a separate question — which brings the third point.

Third: any setting that extends range must be validated against measurement in the extended range, not merely observed to converge. Convergence is not correctness. The reason this result is usable is that the extra 2.4° of incidence is also more accurate, and that was demonstrated rather than assumed.
